title: Georgia regulators' Dec 15 decision: how real-time payments split between fuel and base costs
linkText: Larger businesses' real-time power payments and your Georgia Power bill

units.t: The Georgia Public Service Commission (PSC), five commissioners who set utility rates, will decide how much of larger businesses' real-time payments counts toward fuel costs.
Real-time prices change by the hour.
Georgia Power customers on standard rates, including homes.
More real-time money toward fuel would likely lower their fuel charge, the bill's fuel part.
Base rates, the rest of the bill, could rise later.
Written arguments due Dec 2; decision set for Dec 15, 2026; comments due 24 hours before the vote.

P-041.text: DIRECT TESTIMONY OF DR. ROSS BEPPLER, LEE EVANS, AND BRANDON LOONEY IN SUPPORT OF GEORGIA POWER COMPANY’S RTP REVENUE CREDIT AND ALLOCATION METHODOLOGY AUGUST 14, 2026

P-042.text: RTP rates are a collection of tariffs that provide eligible customers the option to take on price risk in exchange for potential cost savings. The Company provides participating customers an hourly price that reflects its expectation of the marginal cost of electricity.

P-043.text: Georgia Power’s RTP tariffs are two-part rate structures that blend standard embedded rates with a marginal cost-based rate. The standard embedded rate is applied to the Customer Baseline Load (“CBL”), while the RTP rate is assessed to incremental load and reflects hourly marginal costs. The standard embedded rate collects variable and fixed costs incurred by the Company while the RTP rate represents the costs that change alongside variations in load.
P-043.note: Removed footnote number 2, which the text layer fuses to the end of the first sentence.

P-044.text: The Company’s RTP tariffs are available to commercial and industrial customers with a minimum demand of 250 kilowatts (“kW”) (RTP-DA) or 5 megawatts (“MW”) (RTP-HA). Currently, there are approximately 2,300 customers on RTP-DA and 170 on RTP-HA.
P-044.note: Rejoined 'RTP-DA', split by a line-end hyphen.

P-045.text: Access to marginal cost-based rates makes RTP a driver of new economic activity and has been an important tool in attracting incremental load to the state. Importantly, as new projects are evaluated, the Company ensures that the expected revenues more than cover the incremental costs to serve new load. Revenues in excess of the incremental cost put downward pressure on rates for all customers.

P-046.locator: pp.10-11, p.10 line 24 to p.11 line 6
P-046.text: In the 2010 rate case, the Commission approved Georgia Power’s proposal to record RTP fuel revenues based on the average marginal replacement fuel costs (rather than the embedded FCR rate) on an hourly basis. This method appropriately records more RTP revenues to fuel when marginal fuel prices are high and less when they are low, which mirrors the concepts behind the RTP rates and better tracks the RTP revenues collected with the marginal fuel costs being incurred. Notably, the implementation of this revised accounting method did not affect the RTP prices paid by customers but rather more appropriately records the revenues received from RTP customers between fuel and base.
P-046.note: Removed the page footer that falls inside this span at the page break.

P-047.text: Q. WOULD CHANGING THE METHODOLOGY FOLLOWING THIS INVESTIGATION CHANGE BASE RATE REVENUE? A. Yes.

P-048.text: For the incremental load priced at RTP, the revenues based on an average hourly marginal replacement fuel cost are recorded to the fuel account. This average hourly marginal replacement fuel cost is based on all Georgia Power generating units running in each hour plus Georgia Power’s share of pool sales or purchases. For the CBL portion of RTP customer load, fuel costs are billed and revenues are collected as applicable at the underlying FCR rate.

P-049.text: The RTP fuel credit is based on marginal replacement fuel costs as the RTP rate reflects the marginal cost of serving incremental load. This does not incorporate fixed fuel costs, which do not vary with changes in demand. Fixed fuel costs are costs that the Company will incur regardless of changes in RTP incremental load and thus cannot be increased or avoided through changes in load priced at RTP. A contribution to fixed costs is made through the capital substitution component as discussed further below. Q. CAN YOU GIVE EXAMPLES OF THESE FIXED COSTS? A. Yes. In the FCR-27 docket, fixed fuel costs related to non-dispatchable PPAs, existing unit FT costs, and FT costs associated with new generation being added to serve large loads and organic growth were identified as examples of fuel expenses not included in the RTP fuel credit calculation.

P-050.text: Non-dispatchable PPAs are those contracts in which the Company has an obligation to pay for the output of the resource when energy is produced regardless of the system’s need or current cost position. These have also been referred to as take-or-pay contracts. These are distinguished from dispatchable PPAs in which the Company can control the output of the resource in response to changes in the marginal costs of the resource or load on the system. The Company’s renewable PPAs including solar, wind, and biomass are currently structured as non-dispatchable. The execution and certification of non-dispatchable PPAs and their associated costs are not driven by large load growth.
P-050.note: Rejoined 'take-or-pay' and 'non-dispatchable', split by line-end hyphens.

P-051.text: Firm Transportation costs are monthly pipeline capacity reservation payments that ensure gas pipeline transportation availability to existing Georgia Power units during all periods. These costs do not include any variable pipeline transportation costs or commodity costs, which are dependent on delivery volume, priced on a volumetric basis, and captured in the marginal replacement fuel costs used in the RTP fuel credit. Q. HOW IS THAT DIFFERENT FROM NEW FT COSTS? A. New FT costs are those payments that Georgia Power incurs to ensure gas availability for new or future generation that is in the Company’s plans. The Company is distinguishing new FT from existing FT in recognition that the growth of large load customers is a primary driver of new FT costs and they may need to be treated differently. As with the non-dispatchable PPAs, existing FT costs are not driven by large load growth.

P-052.text: The RTP price charged to incremental load in all hours has a component, lambda, which is the marginal cost of the marginal unit on the system. In nearly all hours, the marginal running cost is greater than the average running cost of the system, which means that in virtually all periods, RTP incremental load is contributing to fixed costs. The Company has referred to this as the capital substitution component. Further, the CBL portion of an RTP customer’s load captures the fully embedded base and FCR rate, which directly includes the fixed costs. Q. YOU PREVIOUSLY MENTIONED A CAPITAL SUBSTITUTION COMPONENT, CAN YOU ELABORATE? A. Yes. The difference between lambda and the recorded fuel revenue covers two pieces: generation variable O&M and capital substitution. The capital substitution contribution, which is applied to base rates, covers additional fixed costs above the reliability capacity cost associated with resources that support lower fuel costs, including capital costs for baseload or intermediate generation and FT. Q. WHAT IS THE MAGNITUDE OF THAT CAPITAL SUBSTITUTION COMPONENT? A. The amount will vary from year to year based on the spread between the marginal and average running costs of the system and the volume of load that is priced at RTP. The Company performed an analysis based on 2025 actual data and the capital substitution contribution for 2025 was $264 million.
P-052.note: Removed the page footer that falls inside this span at the page break.

P-053.text: Over the past 16 years since the current RTP fuel credit methodology was established, the system has evolved in both the types of fuel expenses incurred and the magnitude of loads served through RTP offerings. In the FCR-27 proceeding, in light of the increase in large load customers served on Georgia Power’s RTP offerings and to ensure such customers pay their share of costs, PIA Staff and intervenors questioned whether the RTP revenues were appropriately allocated between fuel and base rates and recommended the Commission undertake an additional review of the RTP fuel credit and revenue allocation methodology. As demonstrated in the Stipulation ultimately approved in Docket No. 56765, the Company supported and agreed to this subsequent review.

P-054.text: Per the Company’s revised rules and regulations approved by the Commission in 2025, Georgia Power has committed to protect existing customers from bearing any of the costs of adding these large customers. The Company’s approach ensures not only that large load customers pay for their costs but also that all customers benefit from adding them to the system. As previously noted, when revenues exceed the incremental cost to serve, it creates downward pressure on rates for all other customers. These benefits enabled the Company to freeze base rates through 2028 and ensure the incremental revenue from large load customers has downward pressure of at least $102 per year for the typical residential customer using an average of 1,000 kWh per month for years 2029, 2030, and 2031.
P-054.note: Removed footnote number 3, which the text layer fuses to '2025,'.

P-055.text: The revenues Georgia Power receives from large load customers pay for the costs the Company incurs to serve them. The question raised in FCR-27 and continued in this proceeding is whether those RTP revenues are appropriately being divided between fuel and base. Q. IS THE COMPANY PROPOSING ANY MODIFICATIONS TO ITS FUEL COST RECOVERY IN THIS PROCEEDING? A. Yes. The Company proposes that the costs of new FT attributable to large load customers be fully recovered from those customers and not borne by non-large load customers in the FCR clause.

P-056.text: In their FCR-27 testimony filed in Docket No. 56765, PIA Staff showed a 1-CP (coincident peak) allocation of FT costs. The Company agrees with this approach but proposes using a winter CP and basing the allocation on the share of organic versus large load demand growth. This approach is consistent with the capacity need that drove the incremental generation resources and the allocation in the large load cost model.

P-058.text: There are two potential options to address their concern. The first option is to exclude both the costs and the output from non-dispatchable PPAs in the RTP fuel credit calculation. This is consistent with an approach that the RTP fuel credit should be derived from marginal replacement fuel costs. Removing non-dispatchable PPA output (MWh) from the denominator of the RTP fuel credit calculation will increase the RTP fuel credit rate and thus the recording of all RTP revenues to the fuel clause. However, this approach is not based on all Georgia Power generating units running, as originally approved. The second option is to include both the costs and the MWh from non-dispatchable PPAs in the RTP fuel credit calculation. This would break from the marginal fuel cost-based approach approved and in place since 2010 but also result in a larger allocation of RTP revenues to the fuel clause.
P-058.note: Rejoined 'non-dispatchable', split by a line-end hyphen.

P-060.text: My name is Tom J. Newsome. I am the Director of Utility Finance with the Georgia Public Service Commission (“Commission”).

P-061.locator: pp.2-3, why a fuel credit method is needed
P-061.text: Non-RTP customers, like residential and small commercial customers, are subject to separate rates to collect base revenues and fuel revenues. RTP sales are based on a single rate. RTP revenues must be allocated between base revenues and fuel revenues. The RTP Fuel Credit Methodology is used by the Company to calculate how much RTP revenue to allocate to fuel revenues. The remainder of RTP revenues are allocated to base revenues.

P-062.text: Staff had three guidelines. The first guideline is that fuel related costs should correspondingly be matched with fuel revenues to cover those costs. The second is that costs recovered through the fuel clause should be recovered from all customers, and the third is that costs recovered from fuel revenues should be allocated based on energy usage (MWhs).

P-063.locator: pp.3-4, costs left out of the credit
P-063.text: The Company does not include the following costs in the RTP Fuel Credit Methodology calculation. • Natural gas firm transportation • Natural gas storage • Natural gas hedging gains/losses • Natural gas gains/losses on resales • Coal quality penalties and premiums • Coal rail car leases • Coal rail car shortfall/liquidated damages costs • Start-up costs for Purchased Power Agreements (PPAs) • Energy costs associated with non-dispatchable PPAs (Solar, Wind, Biomass, and Qualifying Facilities) • FCR over/under-balance carrying costs • Income Qualified Discount (IQD) • Non-subscription renewables program expenses • Corporate overhead and labor [fn2] Omitting these costs decreases the RTP revenues allocated to fuel revenues and results in non-RTP customers absorbing all these costs. This is inconsistent with Staff’s guideline that costs recovered through the fuel clause should be recovered from all customers.

P-064.locator: p.4, not all costs need be included
P-064.text: Yes; however, Staff does not necessarily expect that all these costs be included in the RTP Fuel Credit Methodology calculation as there are policy and cost causation arguments that suggest some of these costs could be omitted when calculating the RTP revenues credited to the fuel revenues.

P-066.locator: p.7, estimated effect on current fuel rates (as filed; see S07b)
P-066.text: Q. IF STAFF’S RECOMMENDATIONS HAD BEEN IN PLACE DURING 2023 – 2025 WHAT WOULD HAVE BEEN THE IMPACT ON CURRENT (FCR-27) FUEL RATES? A. The additional $329 million of RTP revenues allocated to fuel revenues would have eliminated a $322 million under collected fuel balance. The current FCR-27 rate would have been lower resulting in a decrease in customer bills of approximately $1.35 per month.

P-067.text: [footnote 4] The $1.35 per month savings based on data in the Company’s Docket 3382 monthly fuel report “FCR-27 Over Under Recovery – June 2026 TS Errata.xlsx” and a residential customer that consumes 1,000 kWhs per month.

P-068.text: 1) Monthly RTP Reporting: Staff recommends monthly fuel reporting include sufficient detail on RTP fuel credit rate, mega-watt hour (“MWh”) sales, RTP fuel revenues compared to the average non-RTP fuel rates. The monthly fuel report filed by the Company under Docket 3382 should include a new separate line item in Retail Fuel Revenues section showing RTP sales (MWhs) and RTP revenues. The Company should file a corresponding separate report to show the calculation of RTP revenues credited to fuel revenues, starting no later than January 1, 2027.

P-070.text: The Company acknowledged the growth in new economic development load will mainly be based on RTP pricing.

P-071.text: [footnote 10] New Large Load customers under the TOU-SC tariff have no CBL, pay RTP rates, and have a Monthly Access Charge (“MAC") to ensure incremental fixed cost recovery.

P-072.locator: p.13, the take-or-pay concern and Georgia Power's two options
P-072.text: Staff is concerned the current RTP Fuel Credit Methodology does not include the costs of non-dispatchable PPA contracts, also referred to as Take or Pay contracts, in the calculation of RTP revenues credited to the fuel revenues. This results in less RTP revenue being credited to fuel revenues. The Company recognized this is a problem in this proceeding, and in testimony recommended either excluding both the energy and the costs of non-dispatchable PPAs from the RTP Fuel Credit calculation (Option 1) or including both the energy and the costs associated with non-dispatchable PPAs in the calculation (Option 2).

P-073.text: Staff recommends Option 2, which includes both the energy (MWhs) and costs (dollars) associated with all non-dispatchable PPAs in the Fuel Credit Methodology. This is consistent with the 2010 rate case proposal, which assumed that all Georgia power unit and purchase costs would be included in the calculation.

P-074.text: Option 1 is inconsistent with Staff’s guidelines. All costs should be included when calculating the amount of RTP revenue to allocate to fuel revenues. Option 1 omits non-dispatchable costs from the calculation when the energy from these non-dispatchable resources serve all customers.

P-075.text: Had the Company wanted to use an accurate “marginal” cost RTP Fuel Cost Credit methodology, the Company should have proposed the associated interchange energy rate (“AIER”) for use as the RTP fuel credit methodology.

P-076.text: The Company provided settlement data for 2025, which showed that approximately 9.8 million MWh of non-dispatchable generation was included in the RTP fuel credit calculation,[fn23] while the Company reported that $486 million in associated costs were excluded from the RTP fuel credit calculation.[fn24] By including MWhs and omitting dollars from take-or-pay contracts in RTP Fuel Credit calculation the Company unreasonably suppressed the amount RTP revenues credited to fuel revenues.

P-077.text: [footnote 24] STF-JKA-3-6. By 2027, the excluded take-or-pay contracts may exceed more 17 million MWh, showing that the impacts of non-dispatchable PPAs are growing. Note, $486 million is the total amount of non-dispatchable costs on the system in the year, not an RTP allocation of cost responsibility.

P-080.locator: p.17, summary of the take-or-pay recommendation
P-080.text: Staff recommends the RTP Fuel Credit Methodology be modified to include both the costs and the energy associated with take-or-pay contracts in the hourly calculation (the Company’s Option 2). These costs are incurred to serve all customers at all times and should be included when the Company calculates the amount of RTP revenues credited to fuel revenues.

P-081.text: Natural gas FT and storage costs are fixed costs the Company pays to ensure natural gas is deliverable via various pipelines and from storage facilities to ensure generating unit reliability.[fn28] These costs are labeled “fixed” because they generally do not change with the volume of natural gas consumed to generate energy. Staff’s investigation noted that RTP customer load occurs in both high and low load hours, making it reasonable that RTP revenues be allocated to the fuel revenues to address the natural gas FT and storage costs.

P-082.text: The Company proposed that only new FT costs be shared and allocated on a winter 1-CP basis. The Company’s proposal does not address the allocation of RTP revenues to fuel revenues to cover existing FT cost. Therefore, the Company’s proposal to allocate new FT costs is only a partial solution and adds undue complexity to the RTP fuel credit methodology.

P-083.text: The Company has asserted that a portion of the revenue paid by RTP customers that is currently credited to base revenues is intended to cover some FT costs.[fn29] This raises the possibility of double recovery because all FT costs are indisputably charged to and recovered from fuel revenues. Absent a modification to the RTP Fuel Methodology, there is a risk that the Company may recover a portion of its FT costs twice.

P-084.text: To eliminate this risk, Staff recommends that the RTP Fuel Credit Methodology be modified so that all FT costs, both existing and new, are allocated across all customers on the basis of monthly energy consumption. Because the FCR tariff rate is an energy-based rate, allocating FT costs on an energy basis is consistent with the manner in which fuel costs are recovered. This is also consistent with how FT costs have been recovered from non-RTP customers over the past 15 years.

P-085.text: It is clear that fixed cost recovery and reliability are not issues limited to a single 1-CP winter hour. FT is necessary for all hours across each month in order to reliably serve customers.

P-086.locator: p.21, alternative if the PSC prefers a demand allocator
P-086.text: If the Commission prefers a demand allocator, or separate treatment of existing and new FT for allocation purposes, Staff recommends that all FT costs no longer be recovered through the FCR mechanism. Instead, these costs should be recovered through base rates to provide full transparency and ensure that costs and revenues are matched within the same recovery mechanism.

P-088.text: Staff recommends that Corporate Overhead costs be included in RTP Fuel Credit calculation, as it is a fuel-related cost and follows procurement.

P-089.text: Staff acknowledges that other costs recovered from fuel revenues are primarily policy-related or could otherwise be considered independent of fuel procurement or dispatch processes. These categories include over/under balance carrying costs, income qualified discount programs, and natural gas hedging gains and losses. It may be reasonable to allocate the three remaining costs in Table 13 to all customers on an energy basis. However these are policy related matters and, Staff makes no recommendation at this time.

P-090.text: However, since the fuel costs are completely the responsibility of ratepayers and the Company has no financial exposure, it is critical to get the RTP fuel credit methodology correct. Any impact to base rates would be a natural consequence of revising the methodology to accurately match costs and cost recovery in the same mechanism. The direction and magnitude of any future impact would need to be determined in a base rate case. Staff reviewed the 2023 – 2025 Annual Surveillance Review filings and concluded the Company would have had the financial capability to absorb additional RTP revenues credited to fuel revenues while maintaining its targeted Return on Equity (“ROE”).

P-091.text: [footnote 45] Staff estimated the Company’s earned ROE would have decreased an average of 0.49 percent during each of these three years. The Company’s revised ROEs would have been 10.3 percent, 10.9 percent and 10.9 percent for 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively. These revised ROEs are well within the Commission approved earnings band of 9.5 percent to 11.9 percent from the 2022 rate case.

P-092.text: My name is John D. Wilson. I am the Vice President of Grid Strategies LLC

P-093.text: ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING IN THIS CASE? A: Georgia Interfaith Power and Light (GIPL), and its member congregations Park Avenue Baptist Church, Temple Sinai, and Unitarian Universalist Church of Savannah.

P-094.text: First, I find that Georgia Power has set its RTP price too low during peak hours because the reliability cost component was set inconsistently with the peaker method.

P-095.text: Second, I find that several categories of costs recovered from FCR customers are not included in the RTP fuel credit. The RTP fuel credit – on a $/MWh basis – is therefore an underestimate of the fuel costs that should be allocated to the incremental load priced at RTP. Accordingly, I make several recommendations for changes to the RTP fuel credit, including that the Commission should: 4. Adopt Georgia Power’s recommendation to “exclude both the costs and the output from non-dispatchable PPAs in the RTP fuel credit calculation.”

P-096.text: 5. Adopt, with modifications, Georgia Power’s recommendation to recover the costs of new firm transportation (FT) cost from large load customers, excluding those costs from the FCR rate. 6. Revise the RTP fuel credit calculation to include direct contributions to FT cost, assuming fixed fuel delivery costs are not included in the marginal value of generation capacity. If that is not the case, then I provide two alternate recommendations whereby the Commission should either allocate FT costs to RTP customers in the fuel docket or move FT costs to base rates. 7. Reject Georgia Power’s proposal for a winter 1CP allocation of new FT cost, instead using the same allocation factor as transmission costs until the issue is fully examined in the next rate case. To the extent that the Commission seeks to rely on Georgia Power’s large load cost model, the Commission should also direct Georgia Power to make a working copy available to intervenors on a basis that addresses commercial sensitivity concerns yet allows for full stakeholder participation in Commission decisions based wholly or in part on that model. 8. Revise the RTP fuel revenue credit to include coal-related costs and corporate overhead and labor.

P-097.text: In the last few years, the Commission has approved the procurement of thousands of megawatts of new generation resources to accommodate large load customers. Given the magnitude of the billpayer investments forecasted by Georgia Power, the Commission has treated these large loads in a distinct manner, holding them to a higher standard when it comes to cost shifting. The FCR-27 proceeding was the first fuel proceeding since the data center boom began and parties raised concerns that the current RTP methodology, which has been applied to data center customers, resulted in higher fuel costs for other customers, in apparent contravention of Georgia Power’s statements that data centers would not be subsidized by existing customers.

P-098.text: Capital substitution is a core component of the peaker method and represents the contribution from lambda to the cost of more efficient generation. As an example, if a utility built all peakers, then system lambda would be approximately equal to average fuel costs, and there would be no surplus to provide capital substitution – but capital substitution would be unnecessary because the marginal cost of generation, based on the peaker cost, would also be covered. This is because the marginal cost of generation is set to cover the full cost of a peaker unit. Thus, if a customer’s energy use is fully priced using RTP, then in theory the RTP rate covers the full cost of that peaker unit. However, Georgia Power does not fully rely on peakers, at some periods the system lambda recovers more revenues than are credited to cover fuel costs. This surplus is needed to cover the higher cost of generation that operates more frequently than peakers (e.g., intermediate units). This is a necessary cost of service, and from an economics perspective does not provide further surplus to represent downward pressure on rates.

P-099.text: Several categories of costs recovered from FCR customers are not included in either the Georgia Power unit costs or the pool purchases/sales cost. The credit – on a $/MWh basis – is therefore an underestimate of the fuel costs that should be allocated to the incremental load priced at RTP. This shifts costs to FCR customers. While in this proceeding, Georgia Power has agreed to make some changes, it argues that the current method is fair, as any revenues that are not recorded as a credit in the FCR are recorded as base revenues, and serve to diminish the revenue requirement for other customers collected through base rates. While I agree with this concept, it neglects two critical factors: cost allocation in the FCR differs from cost allocation in base rates, and the FCR is subject to under- or over-recovery that is carried forward as a balance, which may affect either an FCR filing or a rate case.

P-100.text: Q: DO YOU SUPPORT THIS PROPOSAL? A: Yes. This resolves this problem with the current RTP fuel credit calculation. I would further note that as long as the output from non-dispatchable PPAs remains less than the load from FCR customers, then the net effect of this approach is to assign both the costs and the benefits of non-dispatchable resources to FCR customers. This is appropriate, as incremental RTP load should be assigned the cost of resources that may be dispatched in response to price-sensitive demand.

P-101.text: Yes, but with modifications. I agree with Georgia Power that removing the costs of new FT attributable to large load customers from the FCR clause addresses one problem with the current RTP fuel credit calculation. However, I do not agree that it is reasonable to excuse incremental RTP load from an explicit allocation of FT cost, nor do I agree with the proposed cost allocation factor for FT attributable to large load customers.

P-102.text: Furthermore, even if FT costs are included in Georgia Power’s marginal value data, it does matter where these revenues are credited. Costs in the FCR are allocated on the basis of energy (MWh) and fixed O&M in base rates are generally allocated on the basis of demand (MW). If the ratio of MWh to MW were the same for all classes, I would agree with Georgia Power. But that ratio, of course, varies, meaning that cost allocation outcomes differ depending on whether FT costs are allocated on the basis of energy or demand. To resolve these problems, the Commission should revise the RTP fuel credit calculation to include a direct contribution to FT costs.

P-103.text: And further, Georgia Power’s assertion that its model uses a winter 1CP allocation factor, nor any information on how it is used, is not supported by any available evidence in this or any other related proceeding. Georgia Power has consistently refused to allow intervenors any opportunity whatsoever to review the large load cost model it refers to – not even on a trade secret basis.

P-104.text: Since FT is similar to transmission, in that it is required to meet peak demand conditions whenever and for whatever reason they may occur, I recommend that new FT costs be allocated between large load customers and other growth using the same allocation factor as transmission costs. This decision could be made explicitly provisional until the next rate case when a full review of cost allocation methods relevant to large load customers can be considered.

P-105.text: This will not result in double-recovery, as the rates charged to RTP customers will not change, just the RTP fuel revenue credit. But it will shift revenue credit from base rates to FCR. This will assist in reducing FCR rates for FCR customers, but may increase base rates for those same customers, depending on how other cost allocation questions are handled.

P-106.text: I support excluding fuel-related costs that are not actual costs of fuel (or purchased power) used to generate electricity. This includes gas hedging gains/losses, gas gains/losses on resales, FCR carrying costs, and net renewable program revenues/expenses.

P-117.text: REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF DR. ROSS BEPPLER, LEE EVANS, AND BRANDON LOONEY IN SUPPORT OF GEORGIA POWER COMPANY’S RTP REVENUE CREDIT AND ALLOCATION METHODOLOGY OCTOBER 27, 2026

P-118.text: Specifically, we address PIA Staff’s three overarching guidelines, which serve as the basis for their recommended modifications to the RTP fuel credit methodology. We explain how these three guidelines, which are introduced for the first time in this proceeding as a policy recommendation, are not supported by cost allocation and ratemaking principles and should be given no weight by the Georgia Public Service Commission (the “Commission”).

P-119.text: Regarding non-dispatchable power purchase agreements (“PPAs”), we emphasize our support, alongside GIPL, for Option 1, which preserves the integrity of RTP as a marginal cost-based rate by excluding both the costs and output of non-dispatchable PPAs from the RTP fuel credit calculation.

P-120.text: PIA Staff’s guidelines are new policy recommendations for the Commission’s consideration,[fn2] and are not based on or consistent with cost-allocation best practices, previous Commission policy decisions, or any widely accepted principles, by their own admission.

P-121.text: PIA Staff’s recommendations endeavor to treat RTP load more like non-RTP load in how costs and revenues are allocated. However, the RTP rate is by design a marginal cost-based rate that is not intended to recover all embedded costs. This does not mean that RTP customers do not pay their fair share of system costs or cost to serve. Rather, the pricing for RTP is dynamic and allows participating customers to take on price risk to better manage how and when they use energy. Eligible commercial and industrial customers can respond to price signals and modify their usage on an hourly basis. RTP customers and non-RTP customers are not similarly situated and do not take service on similar rates by design. Efforts to make RTP cost and revenue allocations more like those for non-RTP customers would undermine the effectiveness and competitive value of RTP as a marginal cost-based rate.

P-123.text: The Company would only be double recovering if it was charging customers for FT costs in both fuel and base rates; however, FT costs are charged to fuel and are not included in base revenue requirements.

P-124.locator: section III, revenue on the base side
P-124.text: That said, just because the full cost of FT in fuel is not directly offset by RTP fuel revenue does not mean that RTP customers are not effectively paying their share of fixed costs with the portion of RTP revenue that is allocated to base. To be clear, RTP revenue allocated to base for fixed costs (like FT) through capital substitution or other mechanisms indicates that such RTP revenue is reducing other costs recovered through base rates and effectively lowering the retail cost of service for customers in a base rate case.

P-125.text: PIA Staff now recommends that the Company recover new and existing FT on a megawatt-hour (“MWh”) or energy basis. That recommendation cannot be reconciled with PIA Staff’s own FCR-27 testimony filed just five months ago, in which it allocated FT using a 1-CP allocator, a demand-based method.

P-126.text: As such, energy is not an appropriate allocation factor for FT because FT is fixed, driven by peak demand, and should be treated similarly to other large infrastructure expenses (generation, transmission, distribution) and allocated on a demand basis.

P-127.locator: section III, demand-based allocation and customer protection
P-127.text: The Company’s proposed demand-based allocation for new FT ensures that the RTP revenues booked to fuel will cover the large load causation of the FT cost independent of project materialization since the allocation will be fixed based on the planning assumptions that drove the need. PIA Staff’s recommended energy-based allocation for new FT does not provide this level of customer protection and is inconsistent with the Commission’s approach to customer protection.

P-128.text: As it pertains to non-dispatchable PPAs, the Company presented two options: Option 1 - exclude both the costs and the output (MWh) from non-dispatchable PPAs in the RTP fuel credit calculation. Option 2 - include both the costs and the output (MWh) from non-dispatchable PPAs in the RTP fuel credit calculation. The Company and GIPL recommend the Commission approve Option 1.[fn11] GAM[fn12] and PIA Staff[fn13] agree that Option 1 will increase the amount of RTP revenues credited to fuel.

P-129.text: Option 1 preserves the integrity of RTP as a marginal cost-based rate and is consistent with the foundational principle that the RTP fuel credit should be derived from marginal replacement fuel costs, consistent with marginal cost recovery theory.[fn14] PIA Staff’s preferred option (Option 2) would be a departure from the marginal fuel cost-based approach approved by the Commission and in place since 2010.

P-130.locator: section IV, Option 1 and marginal cost
P-130.text: Similarly, when RTP load does respond to the price signal, the non-dispatchable PPA cost is unable to be avoided by that response; thus, it should not be included in the credit given for demand response or the cost for taking service. Lastly, the benefits of non-dispatchable PPAs, which deliver energy at a fixed price, accrue to FCR customers by reducing average fuel costs when the fixed price is below the marginal fuel cost. RTP load pays the marginal fuel cost and does not directly benefit from the fixed price feature of the non-dispatchable PPA.

P-131.locator: section IV, Staff's other cost categories
P-131.text: As such, the Commission should decline to adopt PIA Staff’s recommendations presented in Table 1 and instead preserve the integrity and structure of the RTP rate design, as proposed by the Company in its direct testimony.

P-132.text: The Company does not believe that PIA Staff’s recommended monthly reporting and MFR modifications are needed and, in some instances, they are not feasible in the requested timeframe.

P-133.text: The current proceeding is appropriately limited to the accounting treatment of the RTP customer revenues between base and fuel. Intervenor testimony that strays into cost allocation, rate design, and changes to the RTP components are changes the Commission can and should review in the context of the Company’s next base rate case.

P-168.text: The discussion surrounding FT costs in this proceeding appears to conflate RTP and the pricing for service applicable to new very large load (i.e., 100 megawatts and larger) customers. However, the only overlap is that these customers may elect to have all or a portion of their load served through RTP. Except for the fact that RTP is a component of the overall cost to serve new very large load customers, the allocation and recovery of FT costs are entirely unrelated to RTP.
